item.title: Methanol substitution suppresses deflagration-excited knock and increases the efficiency of a hydrogen-fuelled CFR engine
item.description: arXiv:2611.17449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knock restricts the performance of hydrogen spark-ignition engines and is usually attributed to end-gas autoignition. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first study in which methanol is used to replace part of the hydrogen in a hydrogen engine at constant fuel energy addition, and it shows that near the knock boundary the limiting oscillation is excited by the deflagration itself, which methanol removes without derating the performance. Port-injected methanol replaced 20--50% of the hydrogen energy in a variable-compression Cooperative Fuel Research engine at 600 rpm and compression ratios of 8--12. With pure hydrogen, oscillation in the 4--15 kHz range began before 10% of the charge had burned in 97--100% of cycles, and its maximum amplitude (MAPO) followed the maximum pressure-rise rate across 2499 cycles (Spearman $\rho=0.94$). Methanol slowed the deflagration: it replaced high-flame-speed hydrogen, cooled the intake by 24--25 K and, at unchanged intake pressure, enleaned the mixture by 10--13%. At 50% methanol, the 10--90% combustion duration lengthened 2.7--3.0-fold, oscillation onset moved 4.5--8.3$^\circ$CA after CA10 and mean MAPO fell by 89--93% although the spark timing was advanced by 13--19$^\circ$CA, and IMEP and indicated thermal efficiency rose by 2.4--7.8%. Methanol was thus worth more than this advance, and at matched CA50 MAPO was still about 90% lower. The measured combustion duration of all 25 data sets scaled with the computed laminar flame speed as $S_L^{-0.58}$ ($R^2=0.99$); fuel replacement accounted for about three quarters of the reduction in $S_L$, and the end-gas autoignition integral stayed below 0.07, against 1 at autoignition. The chamber kept its cylindrical acoustic modes, whose frequencies fell by 8--9%. The trade-off is formaldehyde emissions, which rose five- to sixfold while NO$_x$ fell by 49--85%.
item.dc:creator: Riming Xu, Mebin Panithasan, Xinyang Wang, Giovanni Vorraro, James W. G. Turner

item.title: AI for Parameter Selection in Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization
item.description: arXiv:2611.18307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) methods provide a way to compute molecular ground-state energies, but their accuracy and runtime depend sensitively on configuration choices such as the subspace dimension, propagation timestep, and the allocation of a fixed sampling budget across circuits, for which no formal selection method exists. In this work, we explore whether oracle models can predict the quantum runtime and approximation error from the Hamiltonian and the candidate configuration. Using synthetic Hamiltonians with controllable spectral properties, we show that machine-learned models can map a Hamiltonian directly to the best-ranked configuration within a predefined grid for the SKQD algorithm, validated against classical Krylov propagation, achieving strong rank correlations between true and predicted error and runtime, Spearman $\rho = 0.969$ and $\rho = 0.905$, respectively. Extending the approach to 50 molecular Hamiltonians (20-50 qubits), with reference ground-state energies from classical calculations, we train regressors that predict the simulation error and runtime for a given molecule--configuration pair ahead of execution, and classifiers to distinguish, from 600 SqDRIFT quantum-hardware runs, whether a configuration achieves a ground-state energy within chemical accuracy ($1.6\times10^{-3}$ Ha $\approx 1$ kcal/mol). For the molecular Hamiltonians, the models additionally provide an a priori feasibility and resource estimate, predicting whether a molecule can reach chemical accuracy on current hardware and at what runtime, thus correctly classifying held-out molecules at the molecule level, achieving balanced accuracy 61.8% in-distribution and 100% for five larger held-out molecules.
item.dc:creator: Doriela Grabocka, Dimitrios Christofidellis, Federico Zipoli, Anna van Elst, Patrick Ruch, Antonio Foncubierta-Rodr\'iguez, Siddhartha Mishra, Matteo Manica

item.title: Bond Anharmonicity in a Caged Molecule Probed by Vibronic Core Spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2611.18331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: X-ray absorption spectroscopy and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering at the nitrogen K-edge show that the N$\equiv$N bond in N$_2$@C$_{60}$ is substantially more anharmonic than in free N$_2$, with the ground-state ($X^1\Sigma_g^+$) anharmonic constant $\hbar\omega_e x_e$ a factor of two larger ($3.8\pm0.3$~meV versus $\sim 1.8$~meV) despite an essentially unchanged harmonic frequency. The same enhancement is found across all three vibronic potentials accessible to the experiment---the electronic ground state, the core-excited intermediate state, and the spectator-decay final state---pointing to a common origin rather than an effect specific to one electronic configuration. High-level coupled-cluster calculations of the N$_2$@C$_{60}$ potential energy surface, however, find no significant change in anharmonicity upon encapsulation, ruling out a simple static distortion of the N$\equiv$N bonding potential by the fullerene cage. We propose instead that the dramatic increase in $\hbar\omega_e x_e$ above the gas-phase value -- which, taken literally, would imply an unphysical halving of the N$_2$ dissociation energy - reflects the breakdown of the single-molecule Morse description, as previously invoked to explain anomalous anharmonicities in N$_2$ clusters, and supported by the observation of shifts in the fullerene host's Raman modes.

item.title: Learning and Generating Time Trajectories of Multidimensional Stochastic Processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.17711v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a multidimensional statistics-informed neural network (SINN) framework for learning and generating trajectories of multicomponent stochastic processes. SINN is built upon a deterministic recurrent neural network that takes streams of white-noise sequences as input and generates ensembles of stochastic trajectories whose statistical properties match those of the underlying stochastic dynamics. While SINN has been demonstrated for various one-dimensional non-Markovian processes, extending it to multidimensional processes is essential for real-world applications. Here, we present key developments toward this goal. First, because direct estimation of multivariate probability density functions (PDFs) becomes computationally challenging with increasing dimension, we represent joint-distribution information using collections of one-dimensional PDFs constructed from linear combinations of the process components. Second, to accommodate the larger set of statistical objectives required to characterize multidimensional processes, we adopt a self-adaptive loss-balancing strategy that dynamically weights the components of the total loss function. Third, we introduce a reference-normalized validation framework that interprets statistical discrepancies relative to the finite-sample variability between independent target ensembles. We also investigate the role of the input white-noise dimension in SINN performance. We evaluate the proposed approach using a Langevin benchmark based on two coupled Duffing oscillators and further demonstrate its applicability to the Langevin dynamics of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam chain and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of a lattice Lotka-Volterra model. Our results demonstrate that the multidimensional SINN framework provides a practical approach for modeling multidimensional stochastic dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Xu, Changho Kim, Andy J. Nonaka, Yuanran Zhu

item.title: Spin-adapted sample-based quantum diagonalization with randomized time evolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.18071v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum algorithms based on the classical post-processing of measurement samples have emerged as effective and robust methods to approximate low-energy wavefunctions of many-body quantum systems on present-day and early-fault-tolerant quantum devices. This paper introduces a generic framework for enforcing spin symmetry within these approaches. We tailor this framework to SqDRIFT, a sample-based quantum diagonalization variant that uses the qDRIFT randomized compilation protocol to generate the quantum samples. We discuss how three key components of SqDRIFT (the initial-state preparation, the construction of the time-evolution circuits, and the classical post-processing) can be adapted to incorporate spin symmetry. We show that spin-pure circuits alone are not sufficient, since the sampled determinants generally span a subspace that is not closed under $\hat{S}^2$, and we restore this closure by completing the sampled electronic configurations. In classical simulations of 4-aminobenzonitrile and of an $[\text{Fe}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ model complex, and in experiments on an IBM quantum processor for the oxo-Mn(Salen) complex, this spin-adapted post-processing yields roots that are exact spin eigenfunctions at every subspace size. On hardware, it does so with diagonalized subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than those of the conventional constructions for the same circuit depth.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Barison, Samuele Piccinelli, Alberto Baiardi, Francesco Tacchino, Ivano Tavernelli

item.title: Solution of the Qubit Marginal Problem from Fermionic Representability
item.description: arXiv:2611.18503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Whether local reduced states are compatible with a global quantum state---the quantum marginal problem---is central to quantum information and simulation. Here we present a solution to the ensemble marginal problem for qubits based on the representability theory of fermions. Encoding each qubit as one fermion in two orbitals, we prove that the representable qubit marginals form an exposed face of the set of $N$-representable fermionic reduced density matrices, selected by the vanishing of every site-occupation variance. Complete hierarchies of fermionic representability conditions therefore transfer exactly to qubits. Applications to frustrated Heisenberg and transverse-field Ising rings show that the $(2,3)$-positivity conditions are exact at the Majumdar--Ghosh point and accurate to about 0.5% at criticality. Because the conditions hold for any quantum state, they also provide a framework for mitigating measurement errors on qubit-based quantum devices.
item.dc:creator: David A. Mazziotti

item.title: Compression of virtual spaces in transcorrelated methods via singular value decomposition: application to the G2 set
item.description: arXiv:2608.10658v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a new singular-value-decomposition-based scheme for constructing small virtual spaces out of large basis sets for transcorrelated (TC) calculations, termed SVD-TC. This work builds on the recent finding that the residual basis error in the TC reference energy converges more slowly than that of the correlation energy. Within the new workflow, the post Hartree-Fock TC calculation is performed in a compressed virtual orbital subspace, obtained by projecting the canonical virtual orbitals from a large basis set onto a smaller basis set through singular value decomposition (SVD). This allows us to achieve the high accuracy allowed by the large basis, whilst the bottleneck steps - TC integral calculation and post-HF correlation method such as CCSD(T) - incur the cost of only a small virtual space calculation. The method therefore is highly efficient, whilst avoiding the composite nature of the reference correction method. Using the new scheme, we widen the scope of benchmark-quality TC results into more complex molecules than previously considered: using the G2-1 set of 55 molecules with first- and second-row atoms, we apply SVD-xTC-CCSD(T) to compute atomization energies. We compare our results against the near-exact semistochastic heat-bath configuration interaction (SHCI) reference values and experiment. We find that SVD-xTC-CCSD(T) delivers chemical accuracy already with triple-$\zeta$ basis sets. Finally, we use the quadruple-$\zeta$ results to analyze the accuracy of pseudopotentials within the TC method, and show that pseudopotential TC workflow provides faster basis-set convergence than all-electron TC. We also present timings for computing the atomization energies on G2-1 set, demonstrating the efficiency of our TC workflows.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Cheng, Kristoffer Simula, Johannes Hauskrecht, Evelin Martine Corvid Christlmaier, Daniel Kats, Ali Alavi

item.title: SATE: Transferable Spin-Adapted Neural Wavefunctions
item.description: arXiv:2611.12002v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate prediction of molecular reactivity requires both accurate and computationally efficient description of electron correlation and spin across various molecular geometries and electronic states. We introduce SATE, a spin-adapted transferable neural wavefunction architecture with effective core potentials. SATE combines a transferable neural wavefunction, the spin-adapted antisymmetrization method, and effective core potentials into a single foundation model architecture pretrained on compositions containing selected elements from hydrogen to bromine. After pretraining and adaptation, our model is able to predict 3d transition-metal spin-state gaps, bond dissociation energies, and reaction energies by addressing two key issues. First, including the core potentials into the model allows us to reduce the number of explicitly treated electrons. Second, using spin-adapted antisymmetrization enforces the prescribed total spin by construction. By testing our model with 3d transition metal chemistry, we evaluate our model's description of strong electron correlation and competing electronic states in such compounds. We find that pretraining improves most tested component energies at matched adaptation budgets, while improvements in spin-state gaps, dissociation energies, and reaction energies remain system dependent. Ultimately, our work lays the foundation for more accurate and transferable modeling of molecular systems by combining the computational efficiency of effective core potentials with explicit control over total spin.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Sereda, Pallas Chou, Morris Hsieh, Emerson Hsieh

item.title: DD-03B: Target-level analysis of ligand-protein dissociation pathways reveals ligand-specific exit pathways weakly coupled to binding affinity
item.description: arXiv:2604.06761v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Protein-ligand interactions are conventionally described by a structure and a binding affinity (Kd). Kinetic simulation datasets have grown rapidly, but most analyses remain structure-centred and RMSD-based, and the kinetic information carried by the trajectories is rarely extracted. Here we analyse 766,550 complete dissociation trajectories for 15,540 protein-ligand complexes grouped into 3,687 UniProt accessions. Each trajectory is reduced to a uniform record of 119 descriptors-ligand and structure size, trajectory statistics, the pathway distribution of escape events, and pocket and escape-volume descriptors-so that records from different systems can be compared, joined and searched. This tokenisation shows that the pocket and the ligand act on the same quantity at different levels: the pocket defines the repertoire of exits, and the ligand sets the weights. In open sites the repertoire collapses to one broad mode and affinity tracks ligand size and contact; in confined pockets the exit ensemble splits into several channels whose weights follow ligand size rather than binding affinity. UniProt grouping is a convenient classification above the PDB entry but not the right final unit: two systems illustrate domain separation and degeneracy, and a structural classifier would be preferable. We present the framework as a general analysis paradigm for molecular dynamics trajectory libraries.
item.dc:creator: Maodong Li, Keyu Gao, Yiming Chen, Zhe Wang, Runxiu Wu, Dechin Chen, Zhijun Pan, Yi Isaac Yang

item.title: Quantum optimal control of steady orbits
item.description: arXiv:2606.15383v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Periodically driven dissipative systems can settle into steady orbits - fixed infinite loops on their dynamical manifolds. In quantum mechanics, steady orbits occur in cooling engines, lasers and masers, precision metrology devices, and magnetic resonance. Steady orbits and stroboscopic steady states are a promising target for quantum optimal control, but the numerical complexity is prohibitive: infinite loops defeat state-of-the-art algorithms that use explicit numerical propagation in the time domain. We report a solution to this problem and introduce a numerically efficient quantum optimal control algorithm for steady orbits. We use this algorithm to design microwave pulse sequences that dynamically polarise nuclear spins and enhance their magnetic resonance signals, while taking into account instrumental distortions. Improved performance relative to leading current methods is demonstrated experimentally.
item.dc:creator: Shebha Anandhi Jegadeesan, Yujie Zhao, Robert Hunter, Hassane El Mkami, Maximilian Keitel, Callum Musselwhite, Graham Smith, Guinevere Mathies, Ilya Kuprov

item.title: Intrinsic Wannier Functions for Hamiltonian downfolding
item.description: arXiv:2608.15557v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Downfolding ab initio material band structure into a low-energy subspace spanned by orbitals of specified atomic character, a procedure known as Wannier downfolding, is a common task in the simulation of complex materials. We introduce the Intrinsic Wannier Function (IWF) method to Wannierize bands with given atomic character. The method is non-iterative and requires only a single dimensionless parameter to disentangle bands. In benchmarks on silicon, graphene, and the three-band model of a mercury cuprate, we show that Intrinsic Wannier Functions provide high quality downfolded band structures compared to those from standard approaches such as Maximally Localized Wannier Functions, the Selected Columns of the Density Matrix method, and Projectability-Disentangled Wannier Functions. Further, their straightforward implementation and robustness position Intrinsic Wannier Functions as a general and useful tool for Wannier downfolding in materials electronic structure and in high-throughput applications.
item.dc:creator: Shuoxue Li, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan

item.title: From First Bond to Stable Adhesion: Multivalent Bond Stabilization in Receptor-Mediated Endocytosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.01293v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: After a particle forms its first receptor--ligand bond near a cell membrane, stable attachment often requires a threshold total bond number $m$. This paper develops a biophysical kinetic theory of this post-capture stage. The bond-number dynamics are modeled as a finite birth--death chain on $n=0,1,\dots,m$, where $0$ is loss of all bonds and $m$ is the stabilization threshold. The mesoscopic rates $\lambda_n$ and $\mu_n$ encode the local energy landscape, accessible receptor--ligand pairs, steric and orientational constraints, and cooperative interactions within the growing cluster. The probability of reaching the threshold before losing all bonds is derived in closed form for general rates and, in the constant-rate case, reduces to a geometric series controlled by the kinetic bias ratio $\rho=\mu/\lambda$. The mean time to failure or stabilization follows from a tridiagonal backward equation. Conditioning on successful attachment is treated as a trajectory-selection effect: the conditioned chain is a Doob $h$-transform whose dissociation rate at $n=1$ vanishes, because successful trajectories cannot lose all bonds before stabilization. A minimal interface between the spatial first-capture probability and the bond-number chain is formulated, together with the conditions under which the stable capture probability factorizes into their product. The analysis shows that hitting probabilities constrain only the rate ratios, whereas the absolute rate scale requires time-resolved or dwell-time data. The threshold $m$ is a model-defined stabilization criterion, not a directly measured ligand count. The rates and threshold are effective parameters specified independently or inferred from kinetic data. The theory provides a quantitative framework for interpreting attachment probabilities, lifetimes, and the transition from first bond formation to a model-defined stabilization threshold.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu
